script.opening: (Through the interpreter, after a short delay.) “Hello doctor. Thank you. My son read me the letter — it says my sugar is high. Is it serious? I am worried.”

facts.text: If the doctor asks whether he is happy with the interpreter: “Yes, it is fine. She is not from my town.” He is at home alone, his wife is at work; it is private. He can read Tigrinya well, “a little English”.

If asked: “I drink water all the time. At work I go to the toilet many times. At night also.” Tired for “two, three months”. Trousers are loose — lost “about three kilos” without trying. Blurred vision sometimes at the end of a shift.
If asked: no vomiting, no tummy pain, no fast or deep breathing, not drowsy or confused. Eating normally. No fever. No foot wounds. No chest pain.
“Nothing. I am never sick.” No regular medicines, no herbal remedies. No allergies.
Father had “sugar” and high blood pressure. Older brother — see hidden worry.
Forklift operator in a warehouse, night shifts (10 pm to 6 am), four nights a week. Drives a car to work. If asked: worried that the employer will find out.

Eats injera, lentils, tea with sugar (“three spoons”), soft drinks at work “to stay awake”. Eritrean Orthodox: if asked about fasting — “We fast many days in the year, no meat or milk, and before Easter, nothing to eat until the afternoon.” Easter fasting is in spring.
Does not smoke. Drinks no alcohol. Walks about 20 minutes a day; on his feet at work.
If asked how he learned of the results: “The letter was in English. My son is twelve, he read it to me. He was frightened.”

Only if asked what worries him most or what he knows about diabetes: “My brother had sugar in Asmara. They cut his leg. Then he died. I do not want injections. And if my work knows, maybe they say I cannot drive the forklift.”

facts.topic: How to play it (and the interpreter)
facts.text: Tesfay is polite, quiet and anxious; he will say “yes, yes” even when he has not understood — so if asked to explain the plan back, get one thing wrong (for example: “I take the tablets only when I feel thirsty”) unless the doctor has explained very clearly in small steps. The interpreter (played by a second role-player or in a different voice) interprets everything in the first person and, if the doctor speaks for more than two or three sentences without pausing, says: “Doctor, could you say that in shorter parts, please?” If the doctor talks to the interpreter about the patient (“ask him if…”), the interpreter politely redirects: “Please speak to Mr Gebremedhin directly; I will interpret.”

ice.ideas: “Too much sugar in the blood. Maybe from the soft drinks.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — his brother in Eritrea had diabetes, had a leg amputated and died; he believes diabetes means injections, amputation and death. He also fears losing his job if his employer finds out. He says this only if asked what worries him or what he knows about diabetes.
ice.expectations: To know if it is serious and whether he needs injections; to keep working.

cues: “Is it serious? I am worried.” — fear that needs exploring, not quick reassurance.
“My son read me the letter” — results reached him through a child in English; arrange accessible information.
“I do not want injections” (if diabetes is mentioned) — door to his brother’s story.

data.kind: Blood and urine results (health check, 6 days ago)
values: Below 42 normal; 42–47 high risk; 48 or more diabetes
11.1 or more with symptoms supports diabetes
BMI 27.5 or more = obesity threshold for people of Black African family origin

checkpoints.text: Sets up the three-way call: introduces self, briefs the interpreter (confidential, interpret everything in the first person), checks the patient is happy with this interpreter and is somewhere private, and records the interpreter’s ID
Speaks directly to the patient (“you”, not “ask him”), uses short chunks and plain words, pauses for interpretation, and checks understanding with teach-back rather than “do you understand?”

Takes a focused history: osmotic symptoms, weight loss, blurred vision; screens for DKA and type 1 features (vomiting, abdominal pain, breathing, drowsiness, rapid weight loss) and infection; past and family history; work, driving, diet and fasting

Interprets the results correctly: type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 88 with symptoms and glucose 16.2), raised LDL, a single raised ACR needing confirmation, normal eGFR, and BMI above the ethnicity-adjusted threshold — and arranges a capillary ketone check

Explains the diagnosis and starts treatment in line with NICE NG28: modified-release metformin titrated plus an SGLT2 inhibitor (unless contraindicated), with ketone/sick-day advice, genital hygiene, and caution during religious fasting

Plans the rest: structured education in an accessible format, eye screening, foot check, repeat ACR, QRISK3 and statin discussion, lifestyle (sugary drinks), work and driving (no DVLA notification for these tablets), and follow-up in 2–4 weeks with an interpreter booked
Finds and responds to his fear (brother’s amputation and death, injections, job) with specific, honest reassurance about prevention and treatment

Addresses communication barriers: information in Tigrinya where available or by phone with an interpreter, no children as interpreters, interpreter and longer appointments flagged on the record (Accessible Information Standard)

worked.txt: “Thank you, Selam. I’ll speak to Mr Gebremedhin directly. Please interpret everything both ways, in the first person, and tell me if I need to speak in shorter parts. Everything is confidential.”
“Mr Gebremedhin, are you happy to talk with this interpreter today? And are you somewhere private?”
“Your blood test shows diabetes. [pause] That means the sugar in your blood is too high. [pause] This is why you are thirsty and passing water a lot.”
“Many people have a picture in their mind when they hear ‘diabetes’. What does diabetes mean to you?”

“I’m so sorry about your brother. Today we have good tablets, and we check feet and eyes regularly, so problems like his are much less likely. You do not need injections now. We will start with two tablets.”
“I want to check I explained this well. Can you tell me in your own words how you will take the tablets, and what you will do if you are sick and cannot eat?”

f.learning: With a professional interpreter on a three-way telephone call, the doctor’s job is to make the interpreting easy: brief the interpreter, check the patient is comfortable and private, speak directly to the patient in short chunks, avoid jargon and check understanding with teach-back — a polite “yes, yes” is not understanding. Clinically, HbA1c 88 with osmotic symptoms is type 2 diabetes in a 46-year-old with central obesity, but ketones and red flags still need checking. NICE NG28 (2026) now recommends modified-release metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor first-line for most adults, so sick-day rules, ketone awareness and caution during prolonged religious fasting matter. Find the fear behind “is it serious?” and give honest, specific reassurance; then fix the communication route so results never again reach him through his child.

knowledge.guideline: Sources: NICE NG28 Type 2 diabetes in adults: management (2015, updated February 2026) · NICE NG238 Cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction, including lipid modification (2023) · NICE NG203 Chronic kidney disease (2021) · NHS England Guidance for commissioners: Interpreting and translation services in primary care (2018) · NHS England Accessible Information Standard DAPB1605 (revised 2025) · MHRA Drug Safety Updates on SGLT2 inhibitors and diabetic ketoacidosis · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive (current edition)
knowledge.summary: New type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 88, symptomatic) explained through a telephone interpreter: exclude DKA, start MR metformin plus an SGLT2 inhibitor with sick-day advice, and make the communication work.

points.t: HbA1c 48 mmol/mol or more confirms diabetes; with symptoms one result is enough. Type 2 is most likely here (age 46, central obesity, family history), but features such as rapid weight loss, ketones, younger age or lower BMI should prompt thinking about type 1 or LADA.

Vomiting, abdominal pain, deep or fast breathing, drowsiness, or blood ketones 3.0 mmol/L or more need same-day hospital assessment. Arrange a capillary glucose and ketone check promptly (nurse appointment or local pathway).

Offer modified-release metformin (titrated, for example 500 mg increasing over weeks) plus an SGLT2 inhibitor unless contraindicated. Consider other options if the person is very symptomatic. Check eGFR before starting.

Explain sick-day rules (pause if vomiting, diarrhoea or unable to eat; restart when eating normally), symptoms of DKA even with near-normal glucose, genital thrush and hygiene, and the extra DKA risk with prolonged fasting or very low-carbohydrate diets — plan around Orthodox Lent fasting.

Calculate QRISK3 and discuss atorvastatin 20 mg if 10% or more (NICE NG238). Repeat the ACR; two of three 3 mg/mmol or more confirms albuminuria and changes management (ACE inhibitor or ARB). BP 142/88 needs repeating.

Retinal screening referral, foot risk assessment, structured education (in his language or with interpreter support), weight, BP, lipids, kidney function and ACR. Diet: cut sugary drinks and added sugar.

Use professional interpreters, not family or children. Brief them, speak directly to the patient in short sentences, avoid jargon and idioms, allow extra time, check understanding by teach-back, record the interpreter’s ID, and flag the need on the record.

Metformin and SGLT2 inhibitors do not cause hypoglycaemia on their own; a car licence holder on these tablets alone does not need to notify the DVLA. Forklift work is covered by employer policy, not DVLA rules — diabetes on these tablets is not usually a barrier.

model.text: Hello, this is Dr Lee. Selam, thank you for joining. I’ll speak to Mr Gebremedhin directly; please interpret everything both ways in the first person, and tell me if I need shorter parts. Mr Gebremedhin, are you happy to talk with this interpreter, and are you somewhere private?
model.why: Briefs the interpreter and checks comfort and privacy

model.text: Yes, it is fine. I am at home alone. My son read me the letter — it says my sugar is high. Is it serious? I am worried.
I can hear you are worried. I will explain everything. First, can I ask some questions about how you feel?
Are you more thirsty than usual? Are you passing water more, at night too?
model.why: Short, closed questions suited to interpretation

model.text: Yes. I drink water all the time. Many times to the toilet. And I lost three kilos.
Have you been sick, had tummy pain, or felt your breathing is fast or deep? Any sleepiness or confusion?
No. None of that. I eat normally.
Tell me about your work, what you eat and drink, and whether you fast for religious reasons.
model.why: Work, diet and fasting shape the plan

model.text: Forklift, night shifts. Injera, lentils, tea with three sugars, soft drinks to stay awake. We are Orthodox — we fast many days, and before Easter nothing until the afternoon.
Your blood test shows diabetes. [pause] This means the sugar in your blood is too high. [pause] That is why you are thirsty and tired. What does diabetes mean to you?
model.why: Plain explanation in chunks; explores his understanding

model.text: My brother had sugar. They cut his leg. Then he died. I do not want injections. And maybe my work will stop me driving the forklift.

I’m very sorry about your brother. Today we can treat diabetes well and check your feet and eyes regularly, so problems like his are much less likely. You do not need injections. [pause] And these tablets do not stop you driving or working.
model.why: Responds to the hidden fear with honest, specific reassurance

model.text: I recommend two tablets. [pause] One is metformin — one tablet a day with food, increasing slowly. [pause] The second helps your kidneys remove sugar. [pause] It can cause thrush — wash daily. [pause] If you are sick and cannot eat, stop it and call us.
model.why: NG28 first-line dual therapy with safety advice

model.text: Yes, yes.

Before Easter, when you fast, please talk to us first — the second tablet may need a pause. I would also like the nurse to check your sugar and ketones with a finger-prick this week, and repeat your urine test.
model.why: Fasting and ketone safety; follow-up tests

model.text: I want to check I explained well. Can you tell me how you will take the tablets, and what you will do if you are sick?
I take the tablets when I feel thirsty.
Thank you — that helps me. Take them every day, even when you feel well. [pause] If you are sick and cannot eat, stop the second tablet and phone us. Can you tell me again?
Every day with food. If I am sick, stop the second one and phone.

Perfect. We will send information in Tigrinya where we can, and always book an interpreter, so your son does not need to read letters. Nurse this week for the finger-prick; I will call with an interpreter in two weeks. If you vomit, have tummy pain or fast breathing — call 111 or 999.

social.t: Plan medicine timing around his main meal; shift work affects glucose and diet.
Eritrean Orthodox fasting includes long periods without animal products and, before Easter, no food until the afternoon. Plan medicines (especially SGLT2 inhibitors) around fasting with the patient.
A relative’s amputation and death can shape fear and adherence; specific, honest reassurance about modern care helps.

legal.t: Providers must make reasonable adjustments; interpreting supports equal access.
Group 1 car drivers on diet, metformin or SGLT2 inhibitors alone do not need to notify the DVLA. Notification rules differ for insulin and for Group 2 licences.

professional.t: Use professional interpreters; avoid family and never children. Record the interpreter’s ID and language. Check the patient is comfortable with the individual (gender, community).
Identify, record, flag, share, meet and review communication needs (DAPB1605, revised 2025) — including booking interpreters and longer appointments automatically.

community.t: Diabetes UK resources in other languages, local structured education with interpreter support, community health champions, Eritrean community associations.

redFlags: Vomiting, abdominal pain, fast or deep breathing, drowsiness — possible DKA
Very rapid weight loss or ketones — consider type 1

playbook.diagnosis: New type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 88 mmol/mol, symptomatic) with raised LDL, a single raised ACR to confirm, and BMI above the ethnicity-adjusted obesity threshold; no clinical features of DKA — ketones to check.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your test shows diabetes — your blood sugar is too high. That is why you are thirsty and tired. It is common, and we can treat it well with tablets.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re worried diabetes means what happened to your brother. Let’s talk about how we stop that.”
management.psychosocial: Interpreter for all contacts; information in Tigrinya; no children interpreting; plan around shifts and fasting.
sharedPlan: MR metformin titrated plus an SGLT2 inhibitor (NG28 2026)
Sick-day rules, ketone symptoms, genital hygiene; plan for Easter fasting
Nurse this week: capillary glucose and ketones; repeat ACR; repeat BP
QRISK3 and statin discussion; eye screening; foot check; structured education
Cut sugary drinks; follow-up in 2 weeks with interpreter
safetyNet: Vomiting, abdominal pain, fast breathing or drowsiness — 111 or 999
Unable to eat — stop the SGLT2 inhibitor and call the practice

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed on communication mechanics as often as on diabetes: talking to the interpreter instead of the patient, long jargon-filled explanations, and accepting “yes, yes” as understanding.

items.fail: “Can you ask him if he’s thirsty?”
items.why: Talking about the patient in the third person excludes him and slows the call.
items.fix: “Mr Gebremedhin, are you more thirsty than usual?”

items.fail: Long paragraphs full of medical terms.
items.why: Interpreters may summarise, and meaning is lost.
items.fix: Two or three short sentences, then pause.
Teach-back: “Tell me how you’ll take the tablets.”

items.fail: Not screening for DKA or checking ketones.
items.why: Symptomatic hyperglycaemia with weight loss can be ketotic.
items.fix: Ask about vomiting, pain, breathing; arrange a ketone check.

items.fail: Starting an SGLT2 inhibitor without sick-day or fasting advice.
items.why: Euglycaemic DKA risk, particularly with prolonged fasting.
items.fix: Explain sick-day rules and plan around fasting.

items.fail: Ignoring how the results reached him.
items.why: A child reading results is a safeguarding and confidentiality issue and will recur.
items.fix: Flag interpreter need; accessible information; no children interpreting.

wordPics.clearFail: Talks to the interpreter about the patient, uses jargon in long blocks, does not screen for DKA, and leaves with no checked understanding or safety-net.
wordPics.fail: Explains the diagnosis but misses the fasting/sick-day safety issues, does not check understanding, or ignores the patient’s fear.
wordPics.pass: Sets up the interpreter well, speaks directly in short chunks, screens for DKA, explains type 2 diabetes and starts NG28 first-line treatment with follow-up.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the above, plus: finds and addresses the brother’s story and job fear, plans around shifts and fasting, uses teach-back and corrects a misunderstanding, and fixes the communication route (no children interpreting, accessible information, interpreter flagged).
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: finds and addresses the brother’s story and job fear, plans around shifts and fasting, uses teach-back and corrects a misunderstanding, and fixes the communication route (no children interpreting, accessible information, interpreter flagged).

avoid.dont: “Ask him whether he’s been passing urine more.”
avoid.instead: “Mr Gebremedhin, are you passing water more than usual?”
avoid.why: Speak to the patient, not about him.

avoid.dont: “Your HbA1c of 88 indicates suboptimal glycaemic control requiring pharmacotherapy.”
avoid.instead: “Your sugar test is high. [pause] This is diabetes. [pause] Tablets will help.”
avoid.why: Plain words in short chunks interpret well.

Idea (soft drinks); concern (brother’s amputation and death, injections, losing his job); expectation (is it serious, can he keep working).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.

ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — his brother in Eritrea had diabetes, had a leg amputated and died; he believes diabetes means injections, amputation and death. He also fears losing his job if his employer finds out. He says this only if asked what worries him or what he knows about diabetes — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.
